faq.question: How does TB-500 differ from BPC-157 mechanistically?
faq.answer: TB-500 works via G-actin sequestration — binding monomeric actin to regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and cell migration. BPC-157 works via VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, GH receptor upregulation, and NO modulation. They are complementary: TB-500 mobilizes cells into wound sites; BPC-157 builds blood supply and growth factor environment. This is the mechanistic basis for their frequent combined use.

faq.question: What's the recommended storage?
faq.answer: 2–8°C, desiccated, protect from light. Powder is hygroscopic — reseal vials after opening. Stable 12–24 months. Post-reconstitution: aliquot into single-use portions in polypropylene tubes, freeze at -20°C. Avoid freeze-thaw cycles.

faq.question: Can you provide full-length Thymosin Beta-4 (43-mer)?
faq.answer: Yes — available on request for protocols requiring the complete 43-amino acid sequence. Higher synthesis complexity and price vs. the TB-500 fragment. Contact us with your requirements.

faq.question: Is TB-500 the same as Thymosin Beta-4?
faq.answer: Not exactly. TB-500 is the synthetic 17-43 fragment of Tβ4, containing the actin-binding domain. The full 43-mer may have additional N-terminal activities. For most tissue repair research, the TB-500 fragment is sufficient — it's the most commonly studied form.
